seoDescription: Explore the process of building a unique acoustic guitar from carbon fiber cloth. This project log covers every step, from creating a foam plug and fiberglass mold to laying up plain and twill weave carbon fiber. Learn about vacuum infusion, including release films, breather cloth, and slow-cure resin. Discover how traditional woodworking techniques, like adding maple supports and kerfed linings, are combined with modern composite materials to create a structurally sound, playable instrument with a unique tone.

chapters.title: Creating the Foam Plug
chapters.description: The process begins by shaping a foam plug that will be used to create the guitar body mold.

chapters.title: Preparing and Making the Mold
chapters.description: PVA mold release is applied to the plug before the fiberglass mold is created to prevent sticking.

chapters.title: Demolding and Preparing for Carbon Fiber Layup
chapters.description: The finished mold is revealed, and the various materials for the vacuum infusion process are explained.

chapters.title: Carbon Fiber Layup and Vacuum Infusion
chapters.description: The carbon fiber is laid into the mold with resin, and a vacuum pump is used to press it all together and remove excess resin.

chapters.title: Preparing the Body and Internal Wood Bracing
chapters.description: A maple block for the neck joint, kerfed linings, and struts are prepared to reinforce the carbon fiber body and provide a gluing surface for the top.

chapters.title: Leveling the Body and Attaching the Top
chapters.description: The body's edge is leveled using a large sanding block, and the reinforced carbon fiber top is glued onto the body.

chapters.title: Attaching the Bridge
chapters.description: The ebony bridge is bolted down, rather than just glued, as a precaution due to potential adhesion issues with the carbon fiber top.

chapters.title: Project Reflections and Future Plans
chapters.description: The builder shares his final thoughts on the experimental build, discussing its successes, areas for improvement, and ideas for future carbon fiber guitar projects.

chapters.title: Final Sound Demonstration
chapters.description: A demonstration of the completed carbon fiber acoustic guitar's sound, presented with no added audio effects.

summary:
## Building the Mold
- The process starts with a **foam plug**, which is shaped and smoothed to define the guitar's form.
- The plug is coated in **fiberglass** to create a hard, finished surface.
- Before creating the final mold, the plug is coated with **PVA (Polyvinyl alcohol) mold release** to prevent the mold resin from sticking.
- The final mold is cast over the plug, resulting in a negative impression of the guitar body.

## Carbon Fiber Layup & Vacuum Infusion
- **Materials Used:**
  - **Plain weave carbon fiber:** Used for the exterior surface layer.
  - **Twill weave carbon fiber:** Used for additional structural layers.
  - **Slow-cure resin:** Provides a 30-40 minute work time for the complex layup.
  - **Release film:** A perforated film that prevents other materials from sticking to the final part.
  - **Breather cloth:** A cotton-like fabric that soaks up excess resin pulled out during the vacuum process.
  - **Vacuum bag film:** A plastic film used to create an airtight seal around the entire layup.
- **Process:**
  1. Multiple layers of resin-wetted carbon fiber are laid into the mold.
  2. The release film, breather cloth, and vacuum bag are placed over the layup.
  3. A **vacuum pump** is attached to remove air, pressing the layers against the mold and pulling out excess resin.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The vacuum infusion process is time-sensitive. All materials must be in place and a vacuum must be pulled before the resin begins to set.

## Internal Structure & Assembly
- To add strength and integrate components, **wood reinforcements** are added to the hollow carbon fiber body.
- **Maple Neck Block:** A 3/4" piece of maple is installed to support the neck joint.
- **Kerfed Linings:** Glued around the body's inner perimeter to provide a larger surface area for attaching the top.
- **Top Bracing:** Two maple struts and a maple wedge are glued to the carbon fiber top to support string tension and the bridge.
- **Leveling:** A large, flat sanding block is used to ensure the top edge of the body is perfectly level before gluing on the top.
- **Bridge Installation:** The ebony bridge is **bolted down** as a precaution against potential adhesion failure between the ebony and the carbon fiber surface.

## Project Reflections & Takeaways
- **Experimental Nature:** The build was viewed as an **experiment** with the primary goal of creating a functional instrument.
- **Structural Success:** The finished guitar feels **super solid** and holds its tune well.
- **Sound Profile:** The guitar has a **unique sound**, different from a traditional wooden acoustic. The material is a huge factor in the final sound.
- **Areas for Improvement:**
  - The **neck joint design** could be integrated more cleanly into the carbon fiber body.
  - With the **string-through bridge design**, bolting the bridge might have been unnecessary.
- **Future Possibilities:** Using a mold allows for complete freedom in body shape. A future version might include a fully composite neck.

Right now, I'm just working on getting this foam smooth and shaped to where I want it. Once it's there, I'm going to fiberglass it and try to get a nice finish on it, and this will be my plug that I'll eventually use to make a mold out of. This is going to be a lot different than my typical guitar builds, so I'll try to do my best to explain what I'm doing. But obviously, I can't go into that much detail, otherwise this video would be two hours long. So just try to stay with me here, and I'll try to show what I'm doing and hopefully it will all make sense.

## Preparing and Making the Mold

I'm getting ready to make the mold out of this. Right now, I'm just applying some PVA mold release so that the resin doesn't stick to the plug when I for it.

## Demolding and Preparing for Carbon Fiber Layup

Alright, here's where we're at. Outside of the mold is a bit messy, but the mold surface looks pretty good, actually. I did kind of have to tap the plug to get it removed, but that doesn't really matter because I don't need that anymore. Next up is to cut up some pieces of carbon fiber and get a body laid up.

This is just a plain weave carbon fiber. You're not totally sure what weight it is, but it is pretty thick. I think I'm going to go with this for the body surface that'll be on the outside. This is a twill weave, and I'm going to use this as basically just as additional material layup, but I'll also cut up some small pieces to fill in the spaces that need a little bit more structural integrity. For the layup, I've got some different materials that I'm using. This is like a plastic film that I'll use to wrap everything up in like a bag at the very end. This is... it's just like cotton cloth or something, but it's used to soak up additional resin that gets pulled from the vacuum. And this is a release film so that all of the other material doesn't stick to the body when it cures. I know this is a lot of confusing stuff that probably doesn't make a whole lot of sense yet, but just try to stay with me here and I'll try to show everything.

## Carbon Fiber Layup and Vacuum Infusion

I'm using a slow-cure resin, so I have roughly 30 to 40 minutes right now of work time, but that's going to go by real fast since I have a ton of layers of carbon fiber to lay up. And I also have to get all the fabrics and the film on as well as pull a vacuum before the resin sets.

Alright, camera died while I was laying up the materials and I didn't have enough time to grab another battery, but here it is. I've got the vacuum pulling and everything looks pretty good and pressed down. This is the little outlet that's connected to my vacuum pump over here. I don't have a perfect seal, so I'll probably just run the pump for another few hours until the resin's at least somewhat cured.

## Preparing the Body and Internal Wood Bracing

Got some PVA residue on the body, so I'll have to get that wiped off and then I'm going to start working on building a top for this. Looks good.

I put a 3/4 inch piece of maple in the body here to add support for the neck joint, and it's also going to give more surface area for the top to attach to. These are kerfed linings, and I'm going to glue these up around the entire perimeter of the body, and that's also just going to give something more surface area for the top to glue down to. And lastly, I have these two maple struts that are going to go down the length of the top, and they're going to be inset into this block of wood and that's going to provide some extra support for the string tension and the bridge. I'm actually using a premade neck and neck block for this guitar, and so the neck block just kind of squeezes into this slot here, but I'll get that mounted more permanently later on in the build.

## Leveling the Body and Attaching the Top

So I've got all of the lining in, but the edge of the body isn't completely flat. So what I've come up with is basically just a giant sanding block, and it's just a bunch of sandpaper glued down. So it'll take a while, but it should sand this edge totally flat and I'll have a good surface to glue the top to.

Alright, so I've got these struts glued into place on the top. The next thing I'm adding is this little maple wedge, which is going to give some extra support for where the bridge is going. So I'll get that glued in and then it will be time to get the top glued onto the body.

## Attaching the Bridge

Acoustic guitar fridges aren't typically bolted down, but because I'm a bit worried about the adhesion between the carbon fiber and the ebony bridge, I've decided to bolt it down instead of risking the bridge potentially flying off the entire...

## Project Reflections and Future Plans

Like always, I'll play a demo at the end, but first I want to share a few thoughts on this project. It's not my prettiest guitar by any means, but it is the first acoustic I've done, so I'm actually just happy that it works. It makes noise, which is good. I kind of view this project more as an experiment than an art piece like my other guitars. Structurally, this thing feels super solid. I haven't had any issues with it staying in tune, and it just feels like a regular wooden acoustic guitar.

One thing I really don't like is how the neck joint area looks, and I knew it was going to look like this. I could have designed that better so that the block sits inside of the carbon fiber, but it just would have made the mold a bit more complex. There's a lot of things that I could have changed or done better on this guitar, but I'm cool with how it turned out.

I did stay with the string-through design instead of adding pins, and since I did that, I probably could have gotten away with not bolting the bridge on and just gluing it down. Even though there's a bit of tension still pulling the bridge, it's not nearly what it would have been if I'd used pins instead of string-through.

Another thing you'll notice is that I didn't put any fret dots or markers on. I just decided to keep this guitar super plain and simple. I also don't really use fret markers all that much, especially when playing acoustic. So there are a few companies that make carbon fiber acoustics, but I've never played one before. So the only real sound comparison I have is just a more traditional wooden acoustic. I don't think this guitar sounds fantastic, but I also don't think it sounds that bad. It's... it's got a different sound to it. There are so many factors that go into the sound, especially on an acoustic guitar. Like the wood or the material used to build the guitar is a huge factor. So there's a lot of different things that I could potentially do if I redesigned this to make it sound better.

The cool part about building with carbon fiber is that I can really make this guitar whatever shape I want just because I'm using a mold. So with all that said, I think I will probably revisit the carbon fiber acoustic idea one day and try to do a complete carbon fiber guitar with the neck also being composite and maybe trying some other different things with it. I had a lot of fun building this thing; it was kind of nice to change it up the build process for once. Alright, let's get to the demo. The sound in the demo is straight audio, so there's no editing or effects added. As always, you guys can follow my work on Instagram @Brossart.
